overview.what: A Redis cache is placed in front of session token verification. The public contract of TokenService.verify() is unchanged: same signature, same exceptions, same ordering of checks.
overview.why: Every authenticated request currently makes a Postgres round trip to re-validate a token that was verified milliseconds earlier. At the morning peak this accounts for 40% of queries hitting the database.
overview.risks: A revoked token left in the cache would be accepted as valid. Step 4 handles this; it is the step that deserves the most attention.
overview.out_of_scope: Permission caching, expired-session purging and the OAuth store migration are untouched.

steps.title: A contract before an implementation
steps.role: Defines the interface the cache must satisfy
steps.intro: Before writing anything Redis-specific I pinned down the minimal contract the auth service needs: read, write with a TTL, delete.
steps.detail: Three methods only. Anything absent (pipelines, scan, stats) is deliberately absent so the service cannot come to depend on it.

files.why: A Protocol rather than an abstract base class: tests can pass a plain dict without inheriting anything, and Redis stays a dependency of the infrastructure layer only.

steps.title: Wiring the cache in without changing the public contract
steps.role: The service consults the cache before the database
steps.intro: The cache slots into verify(). Signature, exceptions and check ordering are identical, so an existing caller sees no difference.
steps.detail: The cache is injected by the dependency container rather than constructed inside the service — that is what lets the tests in step 6 pass a fake.

files.why: The cache read happens after signature decoding, not before. A badly signed token must never be used as a lookup key, otherwise the signature stops protecting anything.
watchpoints: The failure path when the cache is unavailable falls back to the database — confirm this against step 5.

hunks.note: The write-back uses the row's remaining TTL, not a fixed one, so the cache entry can never outlive the session.

files.why: The cache is built once at startup and injected. One instance per request would open a Redis connection per request, cancelling the gain we are after.

steps.title: Invalidation on revocation
steps.role: The core risk: a revoked token must stop passing
steps.intro: This is the step to read most carefully. Without it, revoking a session would leave the token valid until the cache entry expired.
steps.detail: I chose immediate deletion over a short TTL. A short TTL narrows the window without closing it, and this needed a guarantee rather than a probability.

files.why: The cache delete runs in the same logical transaction as the database revocation and before returning to the caller: if Redis fails, the revocation fails too and surfaces as an error.
watchpoints: Ordering is deliberate — database first, cache second. Reversed, a crash between the two would leave a revoked token in the cache.
Bulk revocation (log out all devices) loops over jtis; acceptable up to a few dozen sessions, worth a second opinion beyond that.

files.why: drop() completes the contract. A missing key is not an error: revoking a token that was never cached is a normal case.
